titleText.es: Si no entendéis este, no lo busquéis en el Google.
titleText.en: If you don't get this one, don't google it.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish wording uses informal plural forms common in Spain and the deliberately dated phrase el Google.

regions.labelEs: ESTA GENERACIÓN VA A TENER UNA NOSTALGIA UN TANTO EXTRAÑA.

applications.explanationEn: Va changes for the singular generation, a links the pieces, and tener stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Un tanto softens extraña instead of introducing a countable noun; extraña still changes to match the feminine singular nostalgia.

regions.labelEs: QUERIDA, PONGÁMONOS NUESTRAS MEJORES CUENTAS FALSAS, CONECTÉMONOS AL FOROESPACIO PRINCIPAL Y ENGAÑEMOS A LA GENTE PARA QUE VEA LA IMAGEN DE UN ANO DILATADO.

applications.explanationEn: Pongámonos is a group command that includes the speaker, so it expresses a shared suggested action.
Pongamos loses its final s before attached nos, and the written accent preserves the stress.
Nuestras uses the feminine plural form because the owned noun cuentas is feminine and plural.
Conectémonos is a group command that invites the speaker and another person to perform the action together.
Conectemos loses its final s before attached nos, and the written accent keeps the intended stress.
Engañemos is the group-command form used to propose an action by the group that includes the speaker.
A appears before la gente because people are the direct target of engañemos; la gente identifies that human target.
Para que introduces the intended result, and vea is the special purpose form because that seeing is desired rather than stated as a fact.

regions.labelEs: OH, SERÁ COMO EN LOS VIEJOS TIEMPOS.

applications.explanationEn: Será keeps the full dictionary form ser and adds the singular future ending -á.
Como creates the comparison, and en los viejos tiempos names a familiar earlier era.

cards.answerEn: is going to (before a future action)
cards.noteEn: Va normally means ‘goes.’ Before a and an unchanged action verb, it helps express what one person or thing is going to do.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of ir (“to go”), then a, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Ir changes to match the person: voy a means “I am going to,” vas a means “you are going to,” and va a means “he/she is going to.” The final action stays in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form. This pattern expresses a plan, intention, or expected future event.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is going to do something?

cards.answerEn: to (part of ir a + infinitive, going to do something)

cards.promptEs: la broma de internet que recuerda la tira
cards.answerEn: It refers to an infamous early-web shock image that people spread through deceptive links.
cards.noteEn: The characters imagine future nostalgia for an old trolling ritual: using fake profiles and a social forum to trick strangers into opening an explicit image. The title text warns readers not to search for the reference.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins un tanto, ‘somewhat’
cards.noteEn: Inside the softening expression un tanto, un is a fixed part of the phrase rather than an article before a noun.

example.es: La respuesta es un tanto confusa.

cards.questionEn: How can you soften a description to mean ‘somewhat’ or ‘rather’?
cards.answerEn: Put un tanto before the describing word.
cards.noteEn: Un tanto makes a description less absolute. It is often slightly more measured or formal than using un poco, but both can mean ‘somewhat.’ The description still changes normally to match what it describes.

example.es: La explicación es un tanto larga.

cards.answerEn: somewhat; rather (as part of un tanto)
cards.noteEn: Tanto often concerns amount, but the fixed pair un tanto softens a description in much the same way as ‘somewhat’ or ‘rather.’

example.es: El final fue un tanto raro.

cards.noteEn: Pongámonos combines the group command pongamos with nos. The final s disappears before nos, and the written accent keeps the original stress.

cards.promptEs: propuesta para nosotros: hablemos, comamos, vivamos
cards.questionEn: How do you propose an action for a group that includes yourself, like “let's talk”?
cards.answerEn: Use the special “we” proposal form: most -ar verbs take -emos, while most -er and -ir verbs take -amos.
cards.noteEn: Start from the verb's dictionary form, the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Hablar becomes hablemos, comer becomes comamos, and vivir becomes vivamos. Some verbs also change their spelling or base, so learn unfamiliar forms as you meet them.

cards.promptEs: orden de nosotros + nos unido al final
cards.questionEn: How do you say ‘let's…’ with an action that also uses nos?
cards.answerEn: Attach nos to the group-command form, remove the command's final s, and add a written accent when needed to keep the stress.
cards.noteEn: For an action such as sentarse, start with the group command sentemos. Before attaching nos, drop the final s: sentemos + nos becomes sentémonos. The attached nos still refers to the group that includes the speaker.

cards.questionEn: How do you choose the Spanish form of ‘our’ before a noun?
cards.answerEn: Choose nuestro, nuestra, nuestros, or nuestras to match the gender and number of what is owned.
cards.noteEn: The form matches the owned noun, not the owners. Use nuestro before one masculine thing, nuestra before one feminine thing, nuestros before masculine or mixed plural things, and nuestras before feminine plural things.
With a possessive such as nuestras, mejores picks out the best members of a plural group. Without that kind of determiner, the same form can also mean ‘better.’
Conectémonos combines a group command with nos. The final s of conectemos drops before nos, and an accent is written to preserve the stress.
Al is the required contraction of a + el. Spanish writes them as one word whenever both occur together.
Principal identifies the most important or central one. It has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks a specific person as the object
cards.noteEn: Spanish generally places a before a specific person who receives a verb’s action. This “personal a” is not translated as a separate English word.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. Before the masculine article el, a + el contracts to al.

cards.answerEn: so that (before que and a desired result)
cards.noteEn: Before que and a full event, para introduces the purpose of an action. Translate para que together as ‘so that’ or ‘in order that.’

example.es: Hablo despacio para que todos entiendan.
example.en: I speak slowly so that everyone understands.

cards.questionEn: How do you express a purpose when someone or something else carries out the desired result?
cards.answerEn: Use para que, then put the result verb in the special form used for a purpose that is not yet a fact.
cards.noteEn: That special form is called the subjunctive. It appears because the second action is intended or desired, not presented as an established fact. For example, ordinary ve becomes vea, and ordinary viene becomes venga. Use para plus an unchanged action verb instead when the same person performs both actions.

example.es: Dejo una nota para que Ana la vea.
example.en: I leave a note so that Ana sees it.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes para que, ‘so that’
cards.noteEn: Que completes the purpose connector para que before an event with its own person or thing carrying out the action.

example.es: Cierra la puerta para que no entre frío.
example.en: Close the door so that cold air does not come in.

cards.answerEn: they see; they can see (with gente as the Spanish subject)
cards.noteEn: Vea is a special form of ver used when the seeing is a purpose or desired result rather than a stated fact. Although gente refers to people, it is grammatically singular in Spanish, so it takes the singular form vea.

example.es: Abro la ventana para que vea el jardín.
example.en: I open the window so that she can see the garden.

cards.noteEn: Ano without an accent or ñ is an anatomical word. Do not confuse it with año, ‘year,’ which has the distinct letter ñ.
Será is the future form of ser for one person or thing.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.
Unaccented como can introduce the person, thing, or situation used for a comparison. It does not ask “how”; the question word cómo has an accent.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that an experience feels just like an earlier familiar era?
cards.answerEn: Use como en los viejos tiempos, meaning ‘just like old times.’
cards.noteEn: This conventional nostalgic expression compares the present moment with a fondly remembered period. Como supplies the comparison, while los viejos tiempos names the earlier days.

example.es: Volver a jugar juntos fue como en los viejos tiempos.
example.en: Playing together again was just like old times.

cards.noteEn: In expressions about an earlier era, tiempos means the times or days in which something used to happen, not measured timings.
